fathers/maximus-the-confessor/summary: Byzantine monk and the greatest synthesiser of Greek patristic theology, who defended two wills and two energies in Christ against imperial Monothelitism, was mutilated and exiled, and was vindicated by the Third Council of Constantinople (680–681).
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/story:
Two incompatible accounts of Maximus’ early life survive. The Greek Life makes him a Constantinopolitan aristocrat and head of the imperial chancery under Heraclius who became a monk at Chrysopolis around 614; a hostile Syriac Life by George of Resh‘aina makes him a Palestinian of humble birth. Either way, by the 620s he was a monk at Cyzicus, and the Persian advance drove him to North Africa, where he lived from about 630 among refugee monks near Carthage and became the disciple of Sophronius, later patriarch of Jerusalem.

His early works — the Ambigua to John, the Chapters on Love, the Questions to Thalassius and the Mystagogy — gather the whole Greek tradition into one vision. All things were created through the Logos and each bears a logos, a divine intention for its being; the incarnate Word gathers these logoi to himself, so that creation is a cosmic liturgy moving toward deification. Maximus corrected Origenist cosmology (rest–motion–fall) into creation–motion–rest, and read Dionysius and Gregory of Nazianzus in a rigorously Chalcedonian way.

The imperial attempt to reconcile miaphysites with the formula of one energy (633) and then one will in Christ (the Ekthesis of 638) drew him into controversy. In Carthage in 645 he debated the deposed patriarch Pyrrhus and won him over (briefly). With Pope Martin I he prepared the Lateran Synod of 649, which condemned Monothelitism and the imperial Typos of 648.

Arrested in Rome in 653, Maximus was tried in Constantinople in 655, exiled to Bizya, tried again in 662, and had his tongue and right hand cut off so he could neither speak nor write his teaching. Exiled to Lazica on the Black Sea, he died on 13 August 662. The Third Council of Constantinople (680–681) affirmed two natural wills and energies in Christ, vindicating him, though without naming him.

At the centre of his Christology is the distinction between natural will — the human faculty Christ fully assumed — and gnomic will, the hesitating, deliberative will of fallen persons; in Gethsemane Christ’s human will freely consented to the Father’s. He also distinguished the logos of a nature from its tropos, its mode of existence, explaining how the human can be wholly renewed without ceasing to be human. These ideas became central to Orthodox theology and, through Hans Urs von Balthasar’s Cosmic Liturgy (1941), to modern Catholic and ecumenical thought.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/roots/0/te: Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, Cyril of Alexandria and Dionysius are his constant points of reference; the Ambigua resolve difficulties in Gregory and Dionysius.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/roots/1/te: Uses procession and return, participation and logoi, mediated through Dionysius, while rejecting emanationism.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/roots/2/te: Employs Aristotelian and Neoplatonic commentators’ logic of nature, hypostasis, energy and will with technical precision.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/roots/3/te: His ascetic theology builds on Evagrius’ analysis of passions and contemplation, purged of Origenist speculation.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/roots/4/te: His career was a confrontation with imperial religious policy, ending in a dissident monk’s defiance of emperor and patriarch.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/keyTeachin: Christ has two natural wills and two energies, divine and human, united without confusion in one person.
The logoi of creatures pre-exist in the Logos; the cosmos is ordered toward deification.
Deification: ‘God became man so that man might become god’ by grace, as far as God became man by nature.
Distinction of natural will and gnomic will; sin arises in the deliberative will, not in human nature as such.
The church and its liturgy as an image of the cosmos and of the human person.
Love as the fruit of dispassion and the goal of the ascetic life.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/works/0/no: Expositions of difficult passages in Gregory of Nazianzus and Dionysius; his cosmological masterpiece.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/works/1/no: Sixty-five answers on scriptural difficulties, rich in spiritual exegesis.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/works/2/no: Ascetic centuries, later included in the Philokalia.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/works/3/no: The church building and the eucharistic liturgy as images of God, cosmos and soul.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/works/4/no: Record of the Carthage debate defending two wills in Christ.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/works/5/no: Dogmatic treatises and letters against Monenergism and Monothelitism, including the Letter to Marinus on the Filioque.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/doctrineCo: Supplied the theology of two wills and energies defined at Constantinople III (681), completing Chalcedon.
Gave classic form to the doctrine of theosis as the purpose of creation and incarnation.
His theory of the logoi offered a Christocentric account of the meaning of all created things.
His Letter to Marinus explained the Latin Filioque as compatible with ‘through the Son’, a text central to modern Filioque dialogue.
His ascetic chapters became a backbone of Byzantine spirituality and the Philokalia.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/laterInflu: John of Damascus took over his Christology and doctrine of will; Byzantine theology after 681 is unimaginable without him.
Eriugena translated the Ambigua and Questions to Thalassius in the ninth century; Aquinas knew his teaching on Christ’s wills.
Regarded as one of the greatest Orthodox theologians; modern figures such as Staniloae and Zizioulas build on him.
Balthasar’s Cosmic Liturgy (1941) and Lars Thunberg’s Microcosm and Mediator (1965) sparked a broad ecumenical revival.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/reception/: Venerated as a confessor (feasts 21 January and 13 August); a pillar of Orthodox theology.
Venerated as a saint; his alliance with Pope Martin I and the Lateran Synod are cited as witness to Roman orthodoxy.
As a defender of Chalcedonian dyothelitism he is not received by the non-Chalcedonian churches.
Increasingly read by Protestant theologians interested in Christology, theosis and theological anthropology.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/controvers: Monothelite controversy: he defied emperor Constans II and the patriarchs of Constantinople, and was mutilated for it.
His high view of Roman orthodoxy in some letters is debated in Catholic–Orthodox discussions of primacy.
The authenticity of some texts (e.g. parts of the Opuscula and the Life of the Virgin in Georgian) is disputed.
fathers/maximus-the-confessor/quote/text: Love is a good disposition of the soul by which one prefers no being to the knowledge of God.
fathers/bede/summary: Northumbrian monk of Wearmouth–Jarrow whose Ecclesiastical History of the English People (731) is the foundational history of English Christianity and whose works on time-reckoning popularised dating by Anno Domini.
fathers/bede/story:
Bede was born around 673 on lands belonging to the monastery of Wearmouth in Northumbria and was given at the age of seven to its founder, Benedict Biscop. He moved to the sister house of Jarrow (founded 681–682) under Abbot Ceolfrith, and an anonymous Life of Ceolfrith tells of a boy who, with the abbot, alone kept up the singing of the office after plague devastated the community in 686 — probably Bede. He was ordained deacon at nineteen and priest at thirty by John of Beverley, and rarely travelled beyond Northumbria.

Wearmouth–Jarrow possessed one of the finest libraries north of the Alps, built up by Biscop’s journeys to Rome, and its scriptorium produced the Codex Amiatinus, the oldest complete Latin Vulgate Bible. Bede used this library to become the most learned scholar of his age. He tells us that he always took delight in learning, teaching and writing, and at the end of the Ecclesiastical History he lists some thirty works: biblical commentaries, school texts on grammar, metre and figures of speech, saints’ lives and works on chronology.

His biblical commentaries — on Genesis, the Tabernacle, the Temple, Ezra–Nehemiah, Mark, Luke, Acts, the Catholic Epistles and Revelation — compile and digest Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose and Gregory the Great, with a special interest in allegory and the moral formation of preachers. His works on time-reckoning, especially The Reckoning of Time (725), explained the computus for dating Easter, the relation of the moon to the tides, and the six ages of the world; they made dating ‘from the Incarnation of the Lord’ (Anno Domini), devised by Dionysius Exiguus in 525, standard in the West. His calculation of the world’s age, below the traditional figure, provoked a charge of heresy, which he rebutted in his Letter to Plegwin (708).

The Ecclesiastical History of the English People (731) tells the conversion of the English from Gregory the Great’s mission of 597 to Bede’s own day, with the Irish mission from Iona, the Synod of Whitby (664) and the careers of Aidan, Cuthbert, Wilfrid and Hilda. It quotes documents, names its informants and uses AD dating, while presenting miracles as signs of God’s work. In his Letter to Egbert of York (734) he urged reform of lax monasteries and more bishops.

Cuthbert’s Letter on the Death of Bede describes him dying on 25 May 735 while dictating an English translation of John’s Gospel. His relics were later taken to Durham Cathedral. Called ‘Venerable’ by the ninth century, he was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1899 — the only English Doctor.
fathers/bede/roots/0/text: He called himself a follower ‘in the footsteps of the Fathers’ — Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose and Gregory — and drew heavily on Isidore.
fathers/bede/roots/1/text: Formed entirely within a Benedictine-style monastery shaped by Biscop’s Roman models and the Rule of Benedict.
fathers/bede/roots/2/text: Much of his exegesis treats Old Testament texts — Genesis, the Tabernacle, the Temple, Samuel, Ezra — as figures of Christ and the church.
fathers/bede/roots/3/text: Wrote school texts on grammar, metre and tropes, showing Scripture contains all the figures of classical rhetoric.
fathers/bede/roots/4/text: Championed the Roman (Dionysian) Easter reckoning as apostolic against the Irish usage.
fathers/bede/keyTeachings/0: History as the record of God’s providence in a people’s conversion, offering moral examples.
fathers/bede/keyTeachings/1: Christian time: the six ages of the world, AD dating and the correct calculation of Easter as signs of the church’s unity.
fathers/bede/keyTeachings/2: Scripture read literally, typologically and morally to form preachers and teachers.
fathers/bede/keyTeachings/3: The ideal bishop and monk as humble teacher and pastor, modelled on Aidan and Cuthbert.
fathers/bede/keyTeachings/4: The unity of the English church with Rome.
fathers/bede/works/0/title: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
fathers/bede/works/0/note: Foundational history of English Christianity from Roman Britain to 731.
fathers/bede/works/1/title: The Reckoning of Time (De temporum ratione)
fathers/bede/works/1/note: Computus, calendar, tides and world chronicle; popularised AD dating.
fathers/bede/works/3/note: On Genesis, Tabernacle, Temple, Luke, Mark, Acts, Revelation and others.
fathers/bede/works/4/title: Lives of St Cuthbert (prose and verse)
fathers/bede/works/4/note: Hagiography of the bishop of Lindisfarne.
fathers/bede/works/5/note: Programme of church reform for Northumbria.
fathers/bede/doctrineContributions/0/tex: His commentaries transmitted patristic exegesis to the Carolingian and medieval church.
fathers/bede/doctrineContributions/1/tex: His computus fixed the Western method of calculating Easter and Christian time.
fathers/bede/doctrineContributions/2/tex: His scheme of six ages and his commentary on Revelation shaped medieval views of history and the end.
fathers/bede/doctrineContributions/3/tex: His History became the model narrative of a people’s conversion and of Gregory’s adaptive mission policy.
fathers/bede/laterInfluence/0/text: Through his pupil Egbert of York and Egbert’s pupil Alcuin, Bede’s learning reached Charlemagne’s court.
fathers/bede/laterInfluence/1/text: AD dating spread across Europe largely through his works.
fathers/bede/laterInfluence/2/text: Alfred the Great had the History translated into Old English; Bede shaped the very idea of the gens Anglorum.
fathers/bede/laterInfluence/3/text: Reformers such as Matthew Parker and John Foxe read him as a witness to an early English church; others criticised his miracles.
fathers/bede/laterInfluence/4/text: Honoured as the ‘father of English history’ for his use of documents and named informants.
fathers/bede/reception/0/text: Declared a Doctor of the Church by Leo XIII in 1899; feast 25 May.
fathers/bede/reception/1/text: Commemorated on 25 May; honoured as a father of English Christianity.
fathers/bede/reception/2/text: Venerated by many Orthodox as a pre-schism Western saint.
fathers/bede/reception/3/text: Valued as historian and exegete; his miracle stories are read critically.
fathers/bede/controversies/0: Accused of heresy in 708 for revising the age of the world.
fathers/bede/controversies/1: His partisan support for Roman Easter practice and treatment of the Britons and Irish are debated by historians.
fathers/bede/controversies/2: The reliability of the miracles and of his idealised picture of the English church.
fathers/bede/quote/text: I have always taken delight in learning, teaching and writing.
